planting.note: Set out container plants once frost danger has passed; roots resent summer transplant stress

directions: This compact Western Australian shrub produces masses of cup-shaped, fragrant magenta-pink flowers along its stems in late winter and spring, making it a favorite florist cut flower. Grow it in cool, humus-rich, sharply drained soil and give afternoon shade where summers run hot. Pinch tips after the first flush to encourage bushy growth, and avoid heavy phosphorus fertilizer, which boronias dislike. Plants are relatively short-lived, typically performing well for only a handful of years before needing replacement.

planting.note: Start the growth cycle in autumn as nights cool; pot up seedlings into gritty succulent mix

directions: Each pair of swollen, finger-like leaves on this South African mesemb looks uncannily like a bunny's ears, giving the plant its common name. It is a winter grower that sprouts fresh leaf pairs with cooling autumn weather, flowers in late winter, then dries down and drops its leaves to pass summer dormant and nearly leafless. Keep it bone dry during summer rest and resume watering only once new growth appears, since overwatering a dormant plant quickly causes rot. Grow in full sun in a shallow pot with fast-draining mineral soil.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or spring so roots establish before summer drought

directions: This selection of the rare Sierra foothill native bush anemone was chosen for a more compact habit and flowers that open together in a single showy flush rather than trickling open over weeks. Glossy dark green leaves with peeling tan bark set off cup-shaped, fragrant white flowers with golden stamens from late spring into summer. Once established, it tolerates considerable summer dryness and deer pressure, making it a good choice for Mediterranean-climate gardens. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring and keep evenly moist through the first season

directions: Clumps of stiff, jointed, blue-green stems give this South African restio a bold vertical architecture, with papery cream-to-rust bracts sheathing each joint and dark flower clusters at the tips. It is a staple of water-wise fynbos-style and Mediterranean gardens, tolerating both occasional flooding and drought once roots are established. Cut old flowering stems to the base periodically to keep clumps looking fresh. It adapts to a wide range of soil pH and handles light frost into the low 20s F.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings once nights stay reliably above 55F

directions: This variegated sport of the tropical caricature plant splashes green leaves with streaks of pink, cream, and white, giving it its name from the face-like patterns some gardeners see in the markings. Grown as a houseplant or container specimen outside the tropics, it colors up best with bright indirect light or morning sun. Pinch stem tips regularly to keep growth dense and bushy, since unpinched plants become leggy. Protect from temperatures below 50F, as cold quickly causes leaf drop.

planting.note: Anchor stem cuttings in substrate once water temperature holds above 72F

directions: Larger and more vigorous than the common fanwort it is often confused with, this South American stem plant forms feathery, fan-shaped fresh-green underwater leaves that make a lush background in aquariums and warm garden ponds. It needs bright light and warm water to keep its foliage full, since low light quickly causes stems to thin out and lose lower leaves. Trim and replant the tops periodically to maintain density, and keep it in nutrient-rich water with a steady supply of carbon dioxide for best growth. It is strictly a warm-water plant and will not tolerate temperatures below the mid-60s F.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into sharply drained, slightly acidic soil

directions: Fine, needle-like foliage covers this Western Cape fynbos shrub, which is grown chiefly for its round flower heads that open cream and age to a rich red, prized by florists for fresh and dried arrangements. It needs the same sharp drainage and low-phosphorus feeding regime as proteas and other fynbos plants, and resents heavy or waterlogged soils. Cut stems for arrangements as flower heads color up, which also helps keep the shrub compact. Established plants shrug off summer drought but dislike hard frost.

planting.note: Pot seedlings into gritty mineral cactus mix after the last frost and protect from winter wet

directions: Native to the limestone hills of the Chihuahuan Desert, this tiny button cactus is covered so densely in chalky white spines that the green stem beneath is almost hidden. Minute pink flowers ring the crown in late spring, followed by small club-shaped red fruit. Grow it in full sun in an unglazed clay pot with very fast mineral drainage, and keep it nearly dry through winter to prevent rot, since it is far more sensitive to overwatering than larger cactus species. It tolerates brief cold snaps if kept dry but is not reliably frost hardy in wet winter climates.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
Big Bend National Park flora resources (National Park Service)

planting.note: Pot up seedlings in fall as the winter growing season begins; keep dry through summer dormancy

directions: This South African collector's succulent builds a thick, pale, swollen trunk topped by slender, finger-like leaves that it drops each summer to enter dormancy. Fresh leaves and small tubular flowers appear with cooling autumn weather, making it a winter grower like many relatives in its family. Grow it in a shallow pot with mineral, fast-draining soil and withhold water completely once leaves yellow and drop for the season. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from children and pets.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Set out container-grown nursery stock in spring once soil has warmed; this subspecies is the fern-leaved, undivided-leaf form favored in cultivation over the typical species.

directions: This Channel Islands endemic is grown for its peeling cinnamon-red bark and lacy, fern-like evergreen foliage on a narrow conical frame. Plant in fast-draining soil and withhold supplemental water once established, since wet feet are its main cultivation hazard. Flat sprays of small white flowers appear at branch tips in late spring, followed by woody seed capsules. Stake young trees loosely, as they can be top-heavy before the trunk thickens.
sources: Theodore Payne Foundation Native Plant Database

planting.note: Fall sowing lets winter rains trigger germination, mimicking natural chaparral recruitment.

directions: Redshank is a tall, multi-trunked Southern California chaparral shrub named for the shaggy, reddish, ribbon-like bark that peels from its stems. It is deeply rooted and extremely drought tolerant once past its first two summers, making it a good slope-stabilizing choice on dry banks. Needle-like foliage gives it a fine, airy texture distinct from the coarser look of its chamise relative. Avoid summer irrigation near established plants, since it is adapted to bone-dry dormant seasons.
sources: Theodore Payne Foundation Native Plant Database

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in fall or early spring to establish roots before summer drought.

directions: 'Casitas' is a selected, more compact and floriferous form of the gray-leaved California bush mallow, bred for garden use rather than the rangy habit of wild colonies. It produces pale pink, hibiscus-like flowers over a long bloom season from spring into summer and draws abundant native bees. Cut stems back hard every year or two to keep growth dense, since unpruned plants become leggy. It spreads by root suckers, so give it room or confine it where a colonizing habit is wanted for erosion control.

planting.note: Sow in a gritty, fast-draining mix; plants may take many years to reach blooming size.

directions: Newberry's yucca is a smaller, canyon-dwelling relative of chaparral yucca, forming a tight basal rosette of narrow blue-green leaves. Like its better-known cousin it is monocarpic, sending up a single tall flower spike densely packed with white blooms before the rosette dies, leaving offsets behind. Give it sharp drainage and reflected heat similar to its native canyon walls, and keep it bone dry in winter. It is notably cold hardy for a yucca of its range, tolerating temperatures well below freezing.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Divide and transplant established clumps in spring into cool, sheltered, humus-rich beds.

directions: This white-flowered selection of the giant Chatham Island forget-me-not keeps the species' huge, glossy, cabbage-like leaves but trades the usual blue flower heads for clean white ones. It wants cool, humid, maritime conditions and struggles wherever summers are hot and dry, so coastal gardens or heavily shaded, moist borders suit it best. Mulch heavily and keep the crown constantly moist but not waterlogged. Propagate named white-flowered stock by division rather than seed, since seedlings often revert to blue.

planting.note: Plant against a sheltered, shaded wall or trellis with cool, acidic, humus-rich soil.

directions: 'Nash Court' is one of the oldest named selections of Chile's national flower, dating back to Victorian-era English gardens, and is valued for its soft shell-pink, waxy bells marbled with deeper rose veining. Like the species it is a slow, twining evergreen climber that resents root disturbance once settled, so choose its permanent spot carefully. Keep the roots cool and shaded even where the top growth reaches toward the light, and protect from hard frost and drying winds. Acidic, leafy soil with reliable moisture through the growing season keeps the glossy foliage looking its best.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Direct sow outdoors after frost danger has passed; this trailing annual dislikes transplanting.

directions: 'Blue Bird' is a trailing Chilean annual covered all summer in trumpet-shaped flowers of pale blue-violet with a bright white and yellow throat, flowers that close up in shade or evening and reopen in sun. It is well suited to hot, sunny edging, rock gardens, and hanging containers where its sprawling habit can spill over an edge. It tolerates poor, sandy soil and needs little watering once seedlings are established, making it a good low-maintenance filler. Deadheading is unnecessary since spent flowers are quickly hidden by new ones.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in sharply drained soil or pots; keep bone dry through summer dormancy.

directions: 'Leichtlinii' is a paler, historic form of the rare Chilean blue crocus, with sky-blue petals surrounding a glowing white throat rather than the deep solid blue of the typical form. It holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit and is prized by bulb collectors for blooming in late winter when little else is in flower. Grow it in a bulb frame, alpine house, or very sharply drained raised bed, since it is intolerant of summer wet. Where winters are too wet or cold, lift and store corms dry over the dormant season.

planting.note: Start seed in spring in humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil; protect from winter wet.

directions: This refined selection of the Chilean bridal wreath produces slender spikes of pale rose-pink flowers with deeper veining above a tidy rosette of scalloped, oak-like leaves. It blooms over an unusually long season from midsummer into autumn and makes an excellent cut flower that holds up well in arrangements. Grow it in a sheltered border with reliably moist soil, since both drought and waterlogging check its growth. In regions with cold, wet winters, a dry mulch over the crown helps it survive to flower again.

planting.note: Divide and transplant clumps in spring; give room for the arching, fountain-like habit to develop.

directions: 'Tenuis' is a slender-caned, more weeping selection of the clump-forming Chilean mountain bamboo, with widely spaced culms that arch outward in a loose fountain shape rather than growing stiffly upright. Unlike running bamboos it stays in a well-behaved clump, making it suitable for smaller gardens where spreading bamboos would be unwelcome. It prefers humus-rich soil with consistent moisture and benefits from shelter from drying wind. Remove old or damaged culms at the base each year to keep the clump looking fresh.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant in cool, moist, acidic soil in a sheltered, partly shaded site.

directions: Named for the plant collector who gathered its Chilean seed in the early twentieth century, this selection bears larger, more vivid red-orange flowers tipped in yellow than the typical species, set against glossy, holly-like foliage. It carries a long-standing RHS Award of Garden Merit and is a fixture of woodland and shade gardens in mild, moist climates. Give it acidic, well-drained but constantly moist soil and shelter from strong sun and wind, which quickly scorch the leaves. It resents drought and chalky soil equally, so mimic its cool Andean forest origins as closely as possible.
sources: RHS Award of Garden Merit records

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after all frost danger has passed; give room for an arching, scandent habit.

directions: 'Citrina' swaps the brick-red calyces and red petals of the typical Chinese hat plant for chartreuse saucer-shaped calyces centered by clear lemon-yellow tubular flowers, giving a brighter, cheerier effect. It grows as a loose, arching shrub that can be trained on a trellis or left informal as a sprawling hedge in warm climates. Flowering is heaviest from late summer into fall, and plants respond well to a hard pruning afterward to keep growth dense. North of its hardy zones it makes a good large container or conservatory specimen.

planting.note: Plant grafted or cutting-grown stock, since variegation is unreliable from seed.

directions: This variegated selection of the Chinese parasol tree carries the species' bold, maple-like leaves and smooth green bark but splashes the foliage with cream and white dapple, making a striking specimen tree even before its yellow-green summer flower panicles appear. It grows quickly when young and benefits from a sheltered spot out of harsh wind, which can tatter the large leaves. Average garden soil with reasonably even moisture suits it, and little pruning is needed beyond removing any reverted, solid-green shoots. It is deciduous and drops its leaves early, revealing the trunk's striking green bark in winter.

planting.note: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; this selection is noted for improved cold hardiness.

directions: Distributed from UBC Botanical Garden, this hardier selection of the blue evergreen hydrangea relative holds its glossy, dark evergreen foliage through colder winters than typical seed-grown stock. Over summer it bears flat clusters of small starry blue flowers followed by blue berries, giving a hydrangea-like effect on a more compact evergreen frame. Grow it in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in light shade, sheltering it from the harshest winter exposure in its colder hardiness range. Light pruning after flowering keeps the habit neat without sacrificing next season's bloom.

planting.note: Sow or set out in well-drained soil in full sun; established plants resent being moved.

directions: 'Snowtop' pairs the same fern-like, deeply cut foliage and trumpet-shaped blooms as the typical pink hardy gloxinia but produces pure white flowers with a contrasting yellow throat. It emerges late in spring, so mark its location to avoid accidentally digging into the dormant crown. Give it deep, well-drained soil and full sun, with winter protection from excess wet rather than from cold, since the roots are hardier than they look. Deadheading spent stems encourages a longer summer bloom display.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in warm, humid conditions; seedlings need protection until well established.

directions: The Fiji palm is a larger, heavier-trunked relative of the familiar Christmas palm, grown in frost-free tropical and subtropical landscapes for its tall, solitary gray trunk and full, arching crown of feathery fronds. It needs rich, well-drained soil and consistent moisture to grow at its best rate, which is markedly faster than many other feather palms once established. Give it full sun and generous space, since mature specimens become quite large and wide-crowned. It has essentially no cold tolerance, so it is strictly a plant for truly tropical or heated-conservatory conditions.

planting.note: Sow where the roots can stay cool and shaded while the vine climbs into sun; give it a shrub or trellis to scramble through.

directions: This Chilean and Argentine climber uses leaf-tip tendrils to scramble through other shrubs, producing solitary daisy-like flower heads in a soft salmon-pink that resemble a single gazania bloom. Like other mutisias it dislikes root disturbance and performs best when its base is shaded and cool even as the stems climb toward full sun. Grow it through an open shrub or low trellis rather than staking it alone, since it is naturally a sparse, informal climber. Reliable drainage at the root zone is essential, as it is intolerant of waterlogged winter soil.

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts into containers or hanging baskets after frost danger has passed.

directions: 'Lofos Wine Red' is a compact, free-flowering selection of creeping gloxinia bred for hanging baskets and patio containers, bearing large, deep wine-red trumpet flowers continuously from a trailing, heart-leaved vine. It is self-cleaning, dropping spent blooms rather than needing deadheading, which keeps container displays tidy with little upkeep. Give it a rich, well-drained potting mix and regular feeding through the season to sustain its heavy bloom production. As a tender perennial it is usually grown as a warm-season annual outside the mildest climates.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix; grow indoors or in a shaded hanging basket outdoors in summer.

directions: Plush vine gets its name from the velvety, dark green leaves with wine-red undersides that cover its trailing stems in a dense, fuzzy mat. It is grown as a houseplant or hanging basket subject rather than outdoors except in frost-free climates, since it has no cold tolerance. Bright, indirect light keeps the foliage color richest, while direct midday sun can scorch the thin leaves. Keep the soil evenly moist but not soggy, and pinch growing tips occasionally to encourage a fuller, trailing habit.
sources: Kwantlen Polytechnic University School of Horticulture Plant Database

planting.note: Pot the large bulb with its top half exposed; this subspecies grows through winter rather than summer.

directions: This southern African subspecies of the curious climbing onion forms a larger, pale green bulb and sends out longer, more rambling twining stems than the typical form, bearing small white star-shaped flowers. Unlike the commonly grown form, it is a winter grower, so its dormant and active seasons are reversed from typical succulent care expectations. Grow it as a novelty houseplant in a bright window or greenhouse, keeping it nearly dry during its summer rest and watering sparingly while the vine-like stems are actively climbing. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so keep it away from pets and children.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock with ample room for the eventual mature canopy; grows fast with regular moisture.

directions: 'Aptos Blue' is a widely planted selection of coast redwood prized for its dense, blue-green foliage on nearly horizontal branches with distinctive hanging branchlets, giving a softer color than the typical dark green species. It grows quickly in cultivation and, like all coast redwoods, wants consistently moist, deep soil and benefits from the humidity of coastal or irrigated inland sites. Because of its eventual immense size, it is best suited to parks, large properties, or windbreaks rather than small home gardens. Avoid planting where summer drought is severe and unmitigated, since this cultivar performs poorly under prolonged water stress.
sources: Urban Tree Farm Nursery plant catalogue

planting.note: Set small bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in any well-drained soil; the species multiplies aggressively from bulbils and can escape cultivation, so site it where spread is welcome or acceptable.

directions: False garlic produces loose umbels of small, sweetly fragrant, bell-shaped white flowers held above grassy, onion-like foliage that lacks any true onion scent when crushed. Plant the small bulbs shallowly in average, well-drained garden soil in sun to light shade, where they will naturalize readily and return every spring with little care. Because the species spreads prolifically by underground bulbils and self-sown seed, it is best reserved for informal cottage borders, naturalized lawn areas, or contained raised beds rather than tidy formal plantings. Established clumps need no supplemental watering beyond normal rainfall in most climates and settle in as one of the easiest small flowering bulbs to grow.

planting.note: Direct-sow or plant tubestock in autumn into open, grassy ground; the plant dies back to its edible tuber over summer and regrows with the cooler season.

directions: Murnong is a tuberous daisy once a staple food source for Aboriginal communities across southeastern Australia, grown today both as a native wildflower and as a heritage bush-food crop. Each plant forms a rosette of narrow, slightly toothed leaves and sends up slender stems topped with bright yellow, dandelion-like flowers followed by fluffy silver seed heads. The edible, parsnip-flavored taproot swells underground through the cool growing season and is traditionally harvested, roasted, or steamed once the foliage dies back in summer. Grow it in open, well-drained grassland soil in full sun, keeping competing grasses in check, and expect the plant to go dormant and disappear above ground during the hottest months before resprouting with autumn rains.

planting.note: Direct-sow or transplant after soil has warmed well past last frost; bushmint grows quickly in heat and can self-sow readily in warm climates.

directions: Bushmint is a fast-growing, strongly aromatic annual herb with soft, velvety, mint-scented leaves and small lavender-blue flowers held along square stems typical of the mint family. In warm climates it grows rapidly into a sprawling shrub-sized plant by midsummer and is traditionally used across the tropics for teas, traditional remedies, and as a bee and pollinator plant. Grow it in full sun in average, well-drained soil, giving it room to spread since mature plants branch widely; it tolerates heat and poor soil but struggles with cold and wet conditions. Because it self-sows freely and has become naturalized or weedy in parts of the tropics and subtropics, gardeners in warm regions should deadhead or remove spent plants before seed drops if containment is a concern.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops & Plants Products

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring into reliably moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in dappled shade; like the Japanese type, this subspecies resents root disturbance once sited.

directions: Long-stiped disanthus is the mainland Chinese counterpart of the better-known Japanese redbud-leaf disanthus, distinguished botanically by the longer stalks bearing its tiny, dark maroon, spidery autumn flowers. Like its Japanese relative, it carries rounded, heart-shaped leaves that turn simultaneously through shades of claret, orange, and purple in a single remarkable autumn display. It demands the same woodland conditions as the typical species: consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil and shelter from hot afternoon sun and drying wind. Because named stock of this particular subspecies is scarce even among specialist shrub collectors, gardeners who do find it should treat it as a slow-growing, long-term investment piece for a sheltered woodland or shade border rather than a quick landscape filler.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in filtered light in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; this palm tolerates brief light chill better than most feather palms its size.

directions: Dwarf fishtail palm is a clustering, shrub-like palm from the understory forests of the eastern Himalayas, forming a wide, suckering clump of multiple short trunks topped with ragged, fishtail-shaped leaflets. Unlike taller, more tender palms, it tolerates brief cold snaps better than most of its relatives and can handle a light frost once mature, making it a popular choice for collectors pushing palm hardiness limits. Plant it in filtered or partial shade in consistently moist, fertile, well-drained soil, protecting it from harsh direct afternoon sun which can scorch the leaflets. Individual stems are monocarpic and die after flowering and fruiting, but the clump continuously produces new suckers, so the overall plant persists and slowly widens for many years.

planting.note: Plant grafted container or balled stock in spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; stake the leading shoot while young if a taller upright form is wanted, or let it cascade unstaked for a wider mounding shape.

directions: This cultivar selects for the steel-blue needle color of Pseudotsuga menziesii var. glauca combined with a strongly weeping, cascading branch habit, producing a dramatic specimen conifer rather than the towering forest tree of the species. Left unstaked, the central leader still grows upright on its own while side branches drape downward, giving an irregular, sculptural silhouette that becomes more pronounced with age. Staking a young plant for several years can encourage a taller, narrower, waterfall-like form instead of a wide mounding shape. Give it full sun and evenly moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and expect slow but steady growth of roughly a foot or so per year once established, making it a long-term focal point for a conifer collection or large rock garden.

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall onto undisturbed, sandy or gravelly desert soil ahead of winter rains; this annual germinates with cool-season moisture and flowers the following spring.

directions: Fremont's pincushion is one of the most abundant small annual wildflowers of the Mojave and northern Sonoran deserts, carpeting sandy washes and flats with pale pink to white, rounded pincushion-shaped flower heads after a wet winter. Its finely divided gray-green leaves form a low mound beneath wiry flowering stems, and the whole plant completes its life cycle quickly before summer heat arrives. Scatter seed directly onto undisturbed, lean, fast-draining sandy or gravelly soil in fall, since the seed needs winter chill and moisture to break dormancy and germinate. No irrigation is needed beyond natural winter and spring rainfall in its desert range; it is a reliable component of desert wildflower seed mixes and provides an important early food source for desert tortoises and native pollinators.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers in fall in well-drained soil in a sheltered, frost-protected spot; this species is noticeably less cold-hardy than its Mediterranean cousin Dracunculus vulgaris.

directions: This Canary Islands and Madeira endemic is a close relative of the familiar Mediterranean dragon arum, sharing the same dramatic, deeply divided foliage but opening a paler, cream-to-pale-yellow spathe rather than the near-black bloom of its mainland cousin. The unusual flower still relies on a brief carrion-like scent to lure fly pollinators, after which the bold palmate leaves remain decorative through summer before the plant dies back to its tuber. Because it comes from a mild, frost-free island climate, it needs noticeably more winter protection than Dracunculus vulgaris and is best grown in a sheltered microclimate or large container that can be moved under cover in cold spells. Plant tubers in free-draining, humus-rich soil in partial shade and keep lightly moist through the growing season, allowing the foliage to die down naturally and withholding water during summer dormancy.
sources: Kew Science Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; this is a vigorous grower that quickly needs sturdy support or ample ground space.

directions: Black coral pea is a fast, vigorous Western Australian climber prized for its unusual near-black flowers, each marked with a contrasting bright yellow blotch at the base of the standard petal, borne in small clusters through winter and spring. Left to climb, it will quickly cover a fence, trellis, or arbor with dense, dark-green trifoliate foliage; left unsupported, it sprawls into a thick, weed-smothering groundcover instead. It tolerates drought, poor sandy soils, coastal wind, and light frost once established, asking only for full sun and sharp drainage to thrive. Prune hard after flowering to keep its vigorous growth in check, since this species can quickly outgrow small spaces if left unchecked.

planting.note: Scarify and soak seed before sowing, or plant container stock in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; give it generous room since mature trees form an enormous spreading crown.

directions: Timbo is a massive, fast-growing legume tree native to the lowland forests of Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay, Bolivia, and Uruguay, closely related to the better-known Central American guanacaste tree and sharing its coiled, ear-shaped seed pods. It develops a broad, umbrella-like crown of finely divided, fern-like foliage that provides deep shade and supports clusters of small, fluffy white flowers favored by bees. Scarifying and soaking the hard seed coat in warm water speeds germination considerably compared to sowing untreated seed. Reserve it for large, frost-free landscapes in zones 10 and warmer, since it grows quickly into a very large tree and has no tolerance for freezing temperatures, and its extensive root system and pod litter make it unsuitable for small urban lots.
sources: Kew Science Plants of the World Online
Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Tropical Tree Database

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic sandy soil in full to part sun; divide established clumps in winter just as new shoots emerge if propagating vegetatively.

directions: Large thatching reed is a bold, clump-forming restio from the South African fynbos, growing considerably larger and coarser in texture than the more commonly grown Thamnochortus insignis, with thick, unbranched, wiry stems rising from well-developed rhizomes. In its homeland it is harvested along with related restios for traditional roof thatching, but in gardens outside South Africa it is grown purely as a dramatic architectural accent for dry, sunny borders or large containers. Give it lean, sharply drained, sandy soil in full sun and avoid rich, moisture-retentive ground, which shortens its life and encourages rot. Once established it needs very little supplemental water and tolerates drought, wind, and coastal exposure, slowly building into a dense, upright clump over several seasons.

planting.note: Set rooted offsets or nursery divisions in spring once night temperatures stay reliably above the mid-30s; this cross between Billbergia nutans and Cryptanthus bahianus spreads fastest when its shallow root mass is barely covered in gritty, fast-draining soil.

directions: Plant divisions in bright to moderate shade in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; this tough hybrid bromeliad tolerates light freezes down into the mid-20s Fahrenheit, making it one of the few true bromeliads reliable as a perennial groundcover rather than a frost-tender container plant along the Gulf Coast. Its narrow, arching leaves run coppery bronze-red in the center and deepen in color with a little morning sun, while clumps spread steadily by offset to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat under trees or along shaded walkways. It needs almost no supplemental feeding once established and shrugs off short dry spells, making it a low-maintenance substitute for liriope or mondo grass in deep shade beds.

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in rich, well-drained, humus-heavy soil in deep to bright shade; this large understory bromeliad from Brazil's Atlantic Forest needs consistent warmth and should be moved to a sheltered spot or container for winters below the upper 20s.

directions: Grow in deep to bright shade in moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil beneath a tree canopy or on a covered porch; Wittrockia superba is native to the understory of Brazil's Atlantic Forest and is one of the most adaptable terrestrial bromeliads for genuine low-light conditions, unlike many showier bromeliads that demand bright, filtered sun to color up. Mature rosettes of broad, spine-edged leaves can spread to several feet across and hold water in a central cup that should be kept topped off and periodically flushed. In the Gulf South it performs best as a large understory specimen in a protected courtyard or shade bed, since it has little cold tolerance and needs winter protection below zone 10.

planting.note: Set rooted stem cuttings or container plants in spring against a wall, fence, or arbor in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; give it something sturdy to climb since it clings by tendrils and quickly covers vertical surfaces in shaded courtyards.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade against a fence, wall, or arbor; this South African forest vine produces large, glossy, rounded leaves with rust-colored felted undersides that give it a lush, almost tropical look while tolerating far less light than true grape relatives. It climbs by tendrils rather than twining, making it easy to train along a shaded trellis, pergola, or the trunk of an established shade tree where sun-hungry flowering vines would struggle. Small greenish flowers are inconspicuous but are followed by edible (if tart) dark purple grape-like fruit that birds readily take. In zone 9 give it a sheltered north- or east-facing wall, since hard freezes will damage top growth even though the rootstock usually recovers.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in loose, well-drained, organically rich soil in half shade; keep the central cup filled with water and protect from direct midday sun, which scorches the broad leaves.

directions: Grow in half shade in loose, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil beneath open tree canopy; this Brazilian forest-floor bromeliad forms a broad, open rosette of soft green leaves and holds its long-lasting orange-and-white flower spike above the foliage for weeks at a stretch. Unlike sun-tolerant bromeliad relatives such as Neoregelia, Canistrum aurantiacum genuinely needs filtered or dappled shade to avoid leaf scorch, making it a good match for the deep shade under live oaks or beneath a lanai where little else blooms. It is strictly a warm-climate plant with no real cold tolerance, so in zone 9 Gulf gardens it is best grown in a large container that can be moved under cover for winter or planted in an especially protected courtyard bed.

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in bright shade to half-day sun; the stiff, suckering rosettes multiply readily into dense colonies over a few growing seasons.

directions: Site in bright shade to half-day sun in gritty, fast-draining soil; this clump-forming Brazilian bromeliad develops attractive copper-bronze foliage tones when it gets a few hours of direct light but holds up fine in brighter shade with greener leaves and a slightly looser habit. Vigorous underground stolons let a single plant colonize a bed over a couple of seasons, making it a useful textural filler for a partly shaded Gulf Coast border once hostas and ferns are exhausted as options. Its pink-bracted, blue-tipped flower spike emerges from the leaf cup in spring and persists attractively for weeks. It has little frost tolerance, so treat it as a warm-season planting that may need protection or container culture through an unusually cold zone 9 winter.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in loose, well-drained soil in filtered or bright shade; this Bahia, Brazil native develops its best apple-green color and tallest bloom spikes out of direct midday sun.

directions: Grow in filtered or bright shade in loose, well-drained soil beneath open canopy or on a covered patio; Portea kermesina forms a large, open rosette of soft apple-green leaves and sends up a tall, airy branched flower spike in shades of crimson and lavender-blue that rises well above the foliage. It is more diffuse-light tolerant than many showy bromeliads and does not need the intense sun that true-color Neoregelia or Aechmea cultivars demand, making it a good architectural accent for a partly shaded Gulf Coast bed or large container. Because it comes from warm, humid Atlantic Forest habitat in Bahia state, it has essentially no frost tolerance and should be grown as a container specimen or moved to shelter whenever a hard freeze threatens.

subcategory: Georgian endemic hulled winter wheat landrace

planting.note: Sow in early autumn in humid mountain valleys so plants establish before winter and vernalize naturally; it is a tall-strawed hulled wheat that needs threshing equipment or purchase of pre-hulled grain.

directions: Makha is a hexaploid hulled wheat species found nowhere outside Georgia, traditionally grown as a winter crop across the humid mountain districts of Samtskhe-Javakheti and western Georgia. It is notably resistant to the diseases and pests that trouble ordinary wheat in wet climates, and its unusually tall, hollow straw was historically repurposed for thatching, basket weaving, and bedding once the grain was threshed. The grain bakes into a dense, flavorful loaf prized locally despite modest yields, and farmers traditionally harvested it in two stages with a hand thresher because the hull resists easy separation. Because Makha tolerates poor soils and humid conditions better than modern bread wheat, it remains part of ongoing efforts to conserve Georgia's endemic grain diversity.
sources: Emirates Journal of Food and Agriculture

planting.note: Sow as soon as high-altitude soil is workable in spring; traditionally broadcast as a mixed stand with barley or rye, with Dika's taller growth occupying the upper tier of the sowing.

directions: Dika is Georgia's own endemic wheat species, historically sown each spring across mountain farms from roughly 750 to 2000 meters elevation in Samtskhe-Javakheti, Racha, and other highland districts. Farmers traditionally broadcast it mixed with barley or rye in a two-tiered planting, letting Dika's taller stems capture light above the shorter companion grain, a practice that thickened the stand and improved overall bread quality. Its flour bakes into a dense, long-keeping loaf that older Georgian farmers nicknamed the "Mother Wheat," and the crop tolerates poor, rocky mountain soils far better than modern bread wheat varieties. Dika remained the staple grain of Georgia's highest farmed valleys for generations before being displaced by higher-yielding modern cultivars.
sources: Emirates Journal of Food and Agriculture

common_name: Zanduri Wheat (Chelta Zanduri, Georgian Disease-Immune Wheat)

planting.note: Sow in cool, humid highland conditions; Zanduri is confined in its traditional range to the Racha-Lechkhumi valleys and performs poorly in hot, dry lowland climates.

directions: Zanduri is the Georgian name for a hulled wheat population built around Triticum timopheevii, grown almost nowhere else in the world and historically confined to the Racha-Lechkhumi highlands of western Georgia. It is remarkable for a near-complete natural immunity to the rusts, smuts, and powdery mildew that regularly damage other grain crops in the region, a trait so valuable that international breeders later used Zanduri as a source of disease resistance and cytoplasmic male sterility in modern wheat breeding programs worldwide. The plant has bristly leaves and stem joints and a long, narrow, hulled head, and its flour was traditionally reserved for bread baked on special occasions and for honored guests rather than everyday meals. Because its home valleys are cool and humid, Zanduri needs reliable summer moisture and struggles in hot, dry lowland conditions.
sources: Emirates Journal of Food and Agriculture
Bulletin of the Georgian Academy of Sciences

common_name: Kolkhuri Asli Emmer (Colchian Emmer, Georgian Endemic Emmer Wheat)
subcategory: Georgian endemic hulled emmer wheat landrace

planting.note: Sow in fall where it is traditionally grown alongside Makha wheat as a mixed stand in West Georgia's humid lowlands; a hulled grain that requires dehulling before milling.

directions: Kolkhuri Asli, also called Colchian emmer, is a narrow endemic wheat species found only in Georgia and considered a living relic of the ancient farming communities of the Colchis lowlands along the Black Sea coast. It is most often found growing intermixed with Georgia's Makha wheat rather than in pure fields, and it carries a compact, flattened hulled head distinct from ordinary emmer. The species shows strong resistance to the fungal diseases common in West Georgia's humid, high-rainfall climate, yet it also performs well under the hotter, drier conditions of eastern Georgia, giving it unusually wide adaptability for such an ancient grain. Its grain is valued for exceptionally high protein and lysine content, producing a notably nutritious flour even though yields remain modest by modern standards.
sources: Emirates Journal of Food and Agriculture

common_name: Tsiteli Doli Wheat (Georgian Red Doli, Caucasus Rouge)
subcategory: Georgian heirloom red-kerneled bread wheat landrace

planting.note: Sow in fall as a winter bread wheat; tillers prolifically and tolerates heavy, poor soils under either rainfed or irrigated management, with rainfed grain prized for better flavor.

directions: Tsiteli Doli, meaning "red Doli" in Georgian, is a red-kerneled soft bread wheat landrace historically grown across Meskheti, Kakheti, and Svaneti, with each region developing its own local ecotype adapted to very different mountain growing conditions. It was significant enough as a heritage grain that seed was carried to southern France decades ago, where it is still cultivated today under the name "Caucasus Rouge." The wheat tillers prolifically and tolerates heavy, poor soils under both rainfed and irrigated management, though unirrigated grain is prized locally for superior flavor and bread-baking character even though it yields less. Its dough forms the base of traditional Georgian flatbreads baked in a wood-fired purne oven, and the variety remains central to regional efforts to revive Georgia's endemic wheat diversity.
sources: Emirates Journal of Food and Agriculture

common_name: Haykakan Sev Eggplant (Armenian Black Landrace Eggplant)

planting.note: Needs a genuinely long warm season, so start seed early indoors and transplant only once nights stay reliably warm; it matures notably slower than most commercial eggplant hybrids.

directions: Haykakan Sev, meaning "Armenian black," is a dark-skinned eggplant landrace maintained in Armenia's national eggplant germplasm collection and grown on small farms across the Ararat plain and surrounding valleys. Its fruit are glossy, deep purple-black, and elongated, typically needing around 115 to 150 days from germination to first harvest, a notably longer season than most commercial hybrids. Compared with standard local check varieties, Haykakan Sev consistently tests higher in both vitamin C and anthocyanin content, whether eaten fresh or cut into strips and shade-dried for winter use in the traditional Armenian manner. Like other Armenian landrace eggplants, it is valued for dense, less-seedy flesh suited equally to frying, stewing, and the smoky roasted preparations common in the region's cuisine.
sources: Functional Food Science (Scientific Centre of Vegetable and Industrial Crops, Armenia)

common_name: Teghakan Khorovaci Eggplant (Armenian Local Roasting Eggplant)

planting.note: Start indoors well ahead of the last frost and transplant once soil and nights are reliably warm; bred for grilling quality rather than early yield, so it rewards a long, full season.

directions: Teghakan khorovaci, or "local roasting eggplant," is an Armenian landrace singled out in the country's national eggplant germplasm collection specifically for khorovats-style grilling and open-fire roasting, the preparation that gives the variety its name. Its elongated purple-black fruit ranked among the highest in anthocyanin and vitamin C content when tested alongside more than a dozen other Armenian landraces, both fresh and traditionally shade-dried. Plants need a long growing season, commonly 115 to 145 days from germination to first harvest, reflecting generations of selection for flavor and fire-roasted texture rather than earliness. The thick-walled fruit chars well on the outside while the interior collapses into the soft, smoky pulp used in classic Armenian roasted-eggplant spreads and salads.
sources: Functional Food Science (Scientific Centre of Vegetable and Industrial Crops, Armenia)
